# Draft:Islamic conquest of Yemen

The Islamic conquest of Yemen (6 AH / 628 CE) is one of the important Islamic conquests that occurred after Khosrow rejected the invitation of Prophet Muhammad to Islam. It began when the Prophet Muhammad sent an invitation to Khosrow II to embrace Islam, which angered Khosrow, who ordered Khosrow II to instruct Badhan to arrest the Prophet Muhammad.
Background
Rise of the Sasanian Empire
The Sasanian Empire was founded by Ardashir I, who began his revolt in the province of Fars against the declining Parthian Empire in order to restore the glory of the Achaemenid Empire and unify Iran under a single rule.
Ardashir, grandson of Sasan and son of Papak, succeeded in defeating the last Parthian king Artabanus IV at the decisive Battle of Hormozdgan in 224 CE, ending Parthian rule and beginning a new historical era.
After his victory, Ardashir established a strong centralized government in the capital Ctesiphon, adopting a strict religious and political legitimacy that differed greatly from the decentralized feudal system that preceded it.
The Sasanians adopted Zoroastrianism as the official state religion to sanctify their authority and began recording religious texts and constructing major fire temples to strengthen Persian national identity.
This marked the beginning of a golden age lasting four centuries, characterized by intense military rivalry with the Romans and a cultural and architectural renaissance.
Rise of the Rashidun Caliphate
The Rashidun Caliphate began immediately after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in the eleventh year of Hijra, when Muslims faced a critical challenge in selecting a leader to preserve the unity of the emerging Muslim community.
The companions of the Prophet gathered in the Saqifah of Banu Sa'ida in a crucial debate, which resulted in the pledge of allegiance to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq as the first caliph of Islam due to his status and closeness to the Prophet.
This beginning established the principle of shura (consultation) as a governing method, since the Prophet did not explicitly appoint a successor.
This period marked the transition from prophethood and revelation to human governance based on the Qur’an and Sunnah, and the first major challenge was the Ridda wars (Wars of Apostasy), which Abu Bakr successfully suppressed.
Islamic conquest of Yemen
The entry of Islam into Yemen requires deep examination of events that began when the Prophet directed attention toward the south. Yemen was not merely a geographical region but a major cultural and demographic center with strong administrative traditions. The story began when the Prophet sent diplomatic letters to the rulers and tribal leaders of Yemen inviting them to monotheism and alliance with the new Muslim state in Medina.
The first mission was exploratory and missionary in nature, when Khalid ibn al-Walid was sent to Najran and northern Yemen, where he stayed for six months calling people to Islam. However, tribal resistance slowed progress, so the Prophet later sent Ali ibn Abi Talib. to Sana'a, where he met the powerful Hamdan tribe. Ali did not come as a conqueror but as a teacher and messenger, and he recited the Prophet’s letter to them, leading the entire Hamdan tribe to embrace Islam in a single day
At the same time, Badhan, the Persian governor of Sana'a under Khosrow II, played a key role. He sent two men to Medina to bring news about the Prophet, and upon hearing the Prophet’s statement about Khosrow’s death that same night, he verified the news and realized the truth of the prophecy. He then accepted Islam, leading to the peaceful collapse of Sasanian authority in Yemen without bloodshed.
The Prophet then sent Muadh ibn Jabal to teach in the region of al-Jund, and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari to Tihama and Zabid. These scholars established mosques and taught Islamic law, embedding Islam deeply into Yemeni society.
Later, the appearance of al-Aswad al-Ansi, who claimed prophethood, threatened Islamic authority in Yemen, but the established Muslim presence helped eliminate him.
Thus, Islam became firmly rooted in Yemen through diplomacy, prophecy, education, and peaceful political transition. Yemenis later played a major role in early Islamic expansion into Syria, Iraq, and Egypt.
